We hope INCISE can help establish ICS as a practical alternative to fine-tuning in surgical video analysis and other domains with a costly labeling burden.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Xu, Bofang Zheng, Guangyu Meng, Nishchal Sapkota, Xianshi Ma, Xu Cao, Tianjiao Yu, Danny Z Chen

item.title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object. Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details. We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation. To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations. We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories. This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor. On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points. Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision. Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation. Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
item.dc:creator: Guangyu Zhao, Yongchang Zhang, Ruizhang Jiang, Zhihong Yu, Yuhao Zhang, Tao Wu, Qimin Zhou, Kunsong Shi, Haoran Wen, Zeyu Zhang, Yin Li, Kun Zhan, Yiwu Zhong

item.title: Depth-Linked Residual Tokens for Multimodal Retrieval and Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26752v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Iterative architectures such as looped language models improve parameter efficiency and reasoning capacity of transformers, yet their sequential backbone iterations introduce substantial computational latency. Conversely, parallelizable learnable special tokens (such as the register tokens in Vision Transformer) enable efficient single-pass inference, but often suffer from the absence of sequential refinement and exhibit redundant representations across tokens. To address these challenges, we introduce Depth-Linked Residual Tokens (DepThink), an efficient framework designed for multimodal retrieval and generation. Operating within a single pre-filling forward pass, DepThink appends a sequence of K learnable residual tokens whose hidden states are coupled through a lightweight, learnable residual recurrence. This mechanism enables each residual token to progressively capture complementary information missed by preceding tokens. Theoretically, we prove that DepThink provides strictly expanded geometric directional reachability over standard learnable tokens and guarantees a provable one-step descent advantage. We evaluate DepThink across multimodal retrieval and generation tasks. DepThink consistently outperforms learnable-token baselines and matches or exceeds looped architectures across dense (2B, 8B) and sparse mixture-of-experts (30B-A3B) backbones under both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning, while accelerating training by up to 11.9 and inference by 4.3 over looped architectures.
item.dc:creator: Jiangfan Zhang, Wentao Bao, Xian Wu, Xiangjun Fan, Jianpeng Cheng, Jun Xiao

item.title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
item.description: arXiv:2611.26754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.
item.dc:creator: Michael G. Medvedev, Nikolai V. Krivoshchapov, Stepan N. Ostarkov

item.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
item.description: arXiv:2611.26759v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.
item.dc:creator: Trent Eriksen, Celeste Betancur Gutierrez

item.title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
item.description: arXiv:2611.26776v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed El Amine Mokhtari, Matei Mancas, Virginie Vandenbulcke

item.title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.26806v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.
item.dc:creator: Ziqing Wang, Hamid Palangi, Lili Zhao, Kaize Ding

item.title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26809v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.
item.dc:creator: Kaustubh Ponkshe, Gyung Hyun Je, Stefan Taga, Colin Raffel, Martin Jaggi

item.title: Realistic Robustness Evaluation of Tabular Data Driven Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26818v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The increasing adoption of Machine Learning (ML) models in high-stakes applications has raised critical concerns regarding their robustness against adversarial attacks. While extensive research has focused on adversarial example generation in image and text domains, the study of such examples in tabular data remains comparatively limited, despite its widespread use in real-world systems. This work introduces AURORA, a modular, open-source tool for evaluating the robustness of ML models on tabular data classification. It integrates multiple adversarial perturbation methods and evaluation metrics within a unified framework to systematically assess model behavior under adversarial conditions. Central to AURORA is its evaluation report, which focuses on robustness analysis by quantifying performance degradation, comparing the impact of different perturbation strategies, and identifying model vulnerabilities across features and input regions. The report is complemented by visual artifacts that facilitate the interpretability of robustness patterns. Additionally, AURORA incorporates a distance adjustment mechanism that penalizes implausible adversarial samples based on feature-level constraints, ensuring that the robustness assessment remains grounded in realistic perturbations and is therefore more reliable.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Silva, Eva Maia, Jo\~ao Vitorino, Isabel Pra\c{c}a

item.title: Rethinking Full-Weight LoRA with Domain and Task Adapter Scaling for Question Answering over Portuguese Well Drilling Reports
item.description: arXiv:2611.26833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains remains challenging, particularly for technical documents such as Portuguese well drilling reports, where annotated data are scarce and domain adaptation may compromise instruction-following capabilities. Although Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is widely used for parameter-efficient adaptation, its scaling after training remains insufficiently explored. This study investigates the impact of LoRA adapter scaling on question answering over Portuguese drilling reports using Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B. Domain-adaptive pretraining (DAPT) is performed either directly on instruction-tuned models or on their base counterparts, with subsequent adapter transfer, while task-specific adapters are trained on WellQuest, an open-source question-answering dataset derived from Portuguese drilling reports. The two adapters are also combined using complementary weights. Scaling factors ranging from 0.1 to 1.0 are evaluated across multiple training checkpoints using BERTScore. Results show that fractional scaling consistently improves DAPT performance over full-weight application, increasing F1 from 68.8\% to 71.9\% for Qwen2.5-7B and from 63.2\% to 68.5\% for Llama-3.1-8B. QA adapters perform best at high but fractional weights, while base-to-instruct transfer yields better results than direct DAPT on instruct-tuned models. Adapter merging provides a modest improvement for Llama-3.1-8B. Overall, these findings demonstrate that post-training adapter scaling can improve domain adaptation without additional data or training.
item.dc:creator: Luan B. Guerra, Diogo M. Paes, Marcelo N. Grimberg, Arnaldo C. Junior, Wallace Casaca, Lucas C. Ribas

item.title: Non-Expanding Gated Continued Fraction Architecture for Feedforward Layers in Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work has shown that continued fraction inspired neural architectures (CoFrGeNets) can be highly parameter efficient yet performant for language modeling. In this work, we revisit continued fraction-based channel mixing with the goal of improving its performance and simplifying integration into standard pre-training protocols for language models. We achieve this by two simple yet critical contributions: i) we propose a novel non-expanding gated continued fraction inspired architectural component to replace feedforward layers in established language model architectures that may use vanilla multilayer perceptrons or gated linear units or (vanilla/gated) experts in mixture-of-experts (MoE) type architectures. ii) We propose a way to re-implement divisions -- the non-linearity in these architectures -- in terms of logarithms and exponentials. By experimenting on different language modeling architectures such as GPT-2, Llama-3, Mamba-2 and (nano) Llama-MoE we find that our proposed architecture performs similarly or significantly better than the continued fraction architecture proposed in prior work along with having higher throughput. In addition, our re-implementation of divisions makes training of deeper CoFrGeNets stable without the need for incremental training which was proposed in prior work as a means to stabilize training, but added notable complexity to existing large language model training implementations. Code is available at http://github.com/IBM/CoFrNets
item.dc:creator: Amit Dhurandhar, Vijil Chenthamarakshan, Karthikeyan Natesan Ramamurthy, Dennis Wei, Rahul Nair

item.title: Scoliosis5K: Multimodal Gait Analysis via Clip-Conditioned RGB-Silhouette Fusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.26849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Color walking video records body boundary motion alongside clothing folds, surface appearance, and recording-environment cues. To examine what an explicit binary silhouette contributes to participant-level classification of scoliosis-related gait when a classifier already observes the paired color sequence, we construct Scoliosis5K, a multi-site collection of 4,998 corridor-walking sequences across 3,010 participant identifiers in which RGB person crops, binary silhouettes, and two-dimensional poses share each recording identifier and frame index. Our architecture uses each patch's pixel deviation from its clip mean to weight two low-rank query and value updates inside a pretrained RGB encoder, fusing the resulting video representation with a silhouette transformer sequence and regional kernel ridge scores extracted from one native-resolution RGB frame per window. Across 988 participants in five participant-disjoint cross-validation folds and three training seeds, the complete system reaches 83.77% accuracy and 79.91% macro-averaged F1, compared with 83.27% accuracy and 79.56% macro-F1 when the video RGB encoder remains frozen under identical inputs. Zeroing the silhouette vector at fixed weights shifts overall accuracy by only 0.10 percentage points while raising positive-category recall from 68.52% to 77.78% and lowering recall for both remaining categories. Macro-averaged AUROC is 0.950 across the cohort and 0.879 among participant pairs matched on acquisition site and recording-count group.
item.dc:creator: Zizhao Peng, Zihan Wang, Zheng Lv, Yan Wang, Ping Li, Fengwei An

item.title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26853v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
item.dc:creator: Sheng Cheng, Deqian Kong

item.title: Coherent Moment Propagation: Epistemic Uncertainty for Pre-trained Robot Policies
item.description: arXiv:2611.26855v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Flow matching policies underpin the state-of-the-art in robot learning, with impressive results ranging from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, they provide no measure of whether their predicted commands can be trusted, particularly in novel situations outside their training set. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the model's weights and quantifies this ignorance, but calculating it at inference time from a flow matching policy is not trivial. Actions are produced by an ODE solver, requiring uncertainty to be propagated through the entire integration process. BayesDiff addresses this problem for diffusion models by propagating the mean and variance of the state through the denoising chain under a last-layer Laplace posterior approximation, but it severely underestimates the epistemic uncertainty. In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff's total variance decays at rate $O(1/T)$ as the number of Euler steps $T$ used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff's variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Saavedra-Ruiz, Anqi Li, Claudia D'Arpino, Alperen Degirmenci, Tucker Hermans, Fabio Ramos

item.title: Your Judge Inherits Your Prompt: In-Context Label Bias in an LLM-as-Judge Is Directional, Not Symmetric
item.description: arXiv:2611.26881v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-as-judge has become a standard way to score open-ended model outputs, yet the judge is itself a frozen language model steered by a few in-context examples, and such models are known to absorb the label balance of their demonstrations rather than treat them as neutral illustrations. We ask whether this label bias reaches an LLM judge used inside a multimodal (video question answering) evaluation pipeline, and what form it takes. Using a fully frozen generator-judge pipeline, we hold the generated answers fixed and vary only the Yes/No balance of the judge's few-shot examples across four demonstration sets. Each verdict is validated against a two-annotator human consensus on 200 examples per dataset. The judge's acceptance rate stays close to human consensus when its examples are balanced or skewed toward rejection, but jumps sharply (by about 30 points on NExT-QA and 20 on MSVD-QA, with a strongly one-sided error profile) when the examples are skewed toward acceptance; the opposite skew produces no matching drop. The bias is therefore one-directional within the tested range of label ratios. A separate five-draw analysis shows that results from a single example draw are unreliable, varying by up to 18 points, more than any difference between prompting conditions. We conclude that demonstration label bias in an LLM judge is a directional, inflation-only failure mode that can fabricate apparent benchmark gains but not losses, and that it is cheaply avoided by balancing the judge's examples and reporting results averaged over several draws.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP, pages 696-706, 2026
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Ahmad, Ahmed J. O. Ahmed, Luca Citi

item.title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments
item.description: arXiv:2611.26897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the surrounding context. Running the agent on these tasks tests whether the same error recurs. ProbeAgent then groups failures with similar causes and generates descriptions that distinguish their errors. This process connects explanations of individual failures to executable tests and descriptions of shared failure modes. We evaluate ProbeAgent across 22 agent configurations using tasks from 10 benchmarks, collecting 1,244 failures and producing 536 failure-mode descriptions. These descriptions distinguish specific errors within broad outcomes such as incomplete work, including planning without acting and stopping before delivering a file. In human evaluation, annotators accept 90.0% of assigned descriptions and correctly reject 83.3% of similar alternatives, supporting the accuracy and specificity of the discovered failure modes.
item.dc:creator: Yue Huang, Yuchen Ma, Shuhang Lin, Yuyang Wu, Zixuan Weng, Zixiang Xu, Xiangqi Wang, Yuexing Hao, Yujun Zhou, Yue Zhao, Olexandr Isayev, Stefan Feuerriegel, Xiangliang Zhang

item.title: Modeling Attributional Style at Scale: A Dataset and Analysis for Psychological Attribution Assessment and Reframing
item.description: arXiv:2611.26900v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: According to the reformulated Learned Helplessness theory, repeated exposure to uncontrollable negative events can foster a depressogenic attributional style, increasing susceptibility to depression yet remaining a tractable target for cognitive therapy. Computational research on attributional cognition, however, is hampered by the lack of large-scale datasets and robust evaluation protocols. In this work, we introduce the Attributional Style Transfer Dataset (ASTD) along with dedicated evaluation metrics, the first benchmark designed to model, assess, and reframe attributional explanations at scale. Constructed via a Prevent-Filter-Validate pipeline that integrates LLM-based generation with specialist validation, ASTD contains 42,000 real-world events paired with psychologically grounded attributions spanning seven styles. Using this dataset, we address two key challenges: (1) scalable assessment of attributional style via both supervised classifiers and zero/few-shot LLMs; and (2) attributional reframing and evaluation, where we propose automatic evaluation metrics to quantify psychological validity. Furthermore, we leverage our proposed metrics to construct a preference dataset, fine-tuning LLMs with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and achieving substantial gains in reframing quality. Together, our dataset, metrics, and methodology offer a new paradigm for understanding and modeling attributional style, with direct implications for scalable and adaptive mental health interventions. Code and data: https://github.com/qzhou711/ASTD
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306:166662-166687, 2026
item.dc:creator: Qiang Zhou, Hanzhen Zhu, Pan Wang, Rui Tu, Huaizhi Qu, Zhuoran Wang, Xin Hu, Lei Li, Tianlong Chen, Jingtong Hu

item.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.26902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
item.dc:creator: Qiang Zhou, Jianing Deng, Siyan Dong, Jingxian Chen, Han-Yi Lin, Jingtong Hu

item.title: AI-Assisted Decision Support for Formula 1 Pit-Stop Strategy: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Programming
item.description: arXiv:2611.26909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pit-stop strategy in Formula 1 is a sequential decision problem under uncertainty, in which strategists decide at each lap whether to pit and which tire compound to fit. We develop a data-driven simulator, calibrated with historical race data, that captures tire degradation, drivers' recent performance, overtaking, yellow flag events, and rivals' pit-stop decisions. We train agents with five Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms and compare them with a Quadratic Mixed-Integer Programming (QMIP) formulation that is optimal in deterministic single-driver settings. Without uncertainty or competition, all DRL methods except TRPO achieve near-optimal performance. With a full grid of competitors and stochastic race events, the ranking of DRL methods depends on the evaluation setting: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and its recurrent variant are the only methods that improve on the QMIP both in fully simulated races and when the actual 2024 races are replayed. Averaged over eight circuits, PPO improves on the QMIP by 0.33 and 0.49 positions in the two settings and Recurrent PPO by less, and in the replay PPO finishes 0.66 positions ahead of the drivers' actual strategies simulated in the same races. The QMIP performs similarly to the other methods, even though it cannot anticipate yellow flag events. Finally, we use the trained PPO policy as a look-ahead decision-support tool that shows the strategist the distribution of race outcomes under each candidate pit-stop action. Applied retrospectively to eight 2024 races, the look-ahead identifies the laps where the actual decision, the recommendation, or a third action was preferable.
item.dc:creator: Felipe M\'endez, Charles Thraves

item.title: ERA: Embed, Route, Adapt for Cold-Start Cross-Model Latent Retrieval
item.description: arXiv:2611.26919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Production retrieval systems are tied to the embedding model that indexed their corpus. Moving queries to a different encoder normally requires re-embedding the whole corpus, and at cold start there are no query logs while every document embedded by the new encoder incurs an API or compute cost. We present ERA (Embed, Route, Adapt), a system for cold-start cross-model latent retrieval. ERA spends a small anchor budget on maximally informative documents, selected from the existing target index via Cosine Farthest Point Sampling, trains a lightweight adapter with a Manifold Alignment Loss that couples directional alignment with orthogonal regularization to prevent representation collapse, and pairs the adapter with a deterministic router that escalates the rare, hard queries that define perceived retrieval quality. Across five BEIR datasets, ERA matches or outperforms point-wise L2 and embedding-conversion baselines, with relative gains of up to 35% nDCG@10 on Arguana, and on clustered corpora its anchor selection also improves prior methods under a fixed anchor budget. With 1.2 ms of adapter and router overhead on top of a ~20 ms local encoder, ERA at a 20% nominal escalation budget reduces end-to-end query latency from roughly 160 ms to 38-86 ms while concentrating escalations on the queries where the projection fails most.
item.dc:creator: Venkata Chivukula, Zifeng Wang, Jinsung Yoon

item.title: Partially canonical axes in large language model representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.26920v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) develop rich internal representations of language, but whether their individual coordinate axes carry meaning, or whether meaning is encoded only in directions in representation space, is still an open question. A common assumption is that individual axes in LLMs are arbitrary. We here challenge this view: across 12 LLMs from six model families, the native axes are reliably more aligned with other models' representations, with human brain responses to language, and with interpretable linguistic features than randomly rotated axes that preserve the same geometry. The native axes nonetheless fall well short of the best achievable alignment, so LLM coordinates are not fully arbitrary but also not fully canonical: they are partially canonical. A theory of how LLMs represent language must explain both the population geometry they learn and why individual units acquire patterns of response profiles that recur across systems.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Gregor de Varda, Ferdinando D'Elia, Greta Tuckute, Evelina Fedorenko, Meenakshi Khosla

item.title: Tokenize Moments, Not Frames: Tokenizer-Aware Budget Allocation for Training-Free Video LLM Acceleration
item.description: arXiv:2611.26933v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video large language models (LLMs) represent each video with thousands of visual tokens, and training-free accelerators that prune or merge these tokens lose accuracy on long videos. Analyzing frame similarity and the vision tokenizers of 16 open models, we trace this loss to a step before token selection. Under a token budget, the frames of a long video are sampled farther apart than the roughly 2 s over which frames remain similar. The two-frame 3D patches of models such as Qwen-VL then blend two unrelated scenes into each visual token, a double exposure that arises before any pruning or merging. Fixed-size tokenizers such as InternVL's avoid this blend but respond differently to the same reduction. We propose ESSENCE, a training-free method that tokenizes moments, segments within which frames remain similar, rather than frames. Before encoding, a closed-form rule uses the sampling interval and the tokenizer class to set the number of token grids and the dimension to reduce; visual tokens are then released from later LLM layers. Against five recent accelerators on Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5, ESSENCE achieves higher accuracy in 58 of 60 comparisons at matched mean time to first token (TTFT). With 80% of the tokens, it matches the average accuracy of the full Qwen models at $1.6\times$ faster TTFT; on GLM-4.1V, it exceeds the full model by up to 3.4 points. Code is available at: https://github.com/zhkandsrz/ESSENCE.
item.dc:creator: Zirui Zhao, Kai Liu, Linghe Kong

item.title: SecretAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Privacy Protection against Vision Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26936v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can infer private information from shared images, including locations, personally identifiable information (PII), and personal attributes such as age and sex, even from medical images. Adversarial perturbations can protect such information against black-box VLMs, but existing methods overlook image quality and introduce visible artifacts into the images they protect. We present SecretAgent, the first general multi-agent framework that protects image privacy against VLMs while preserving visual fidelity. LLM agents iteratively locate the visual evidence that reveals private information and adapt an invisible perturbation to the target VLM's answers and to an appearance reviewer agent, which rejects any candidate with visible artifacts. We instantiate SecretAgent with two complementary variants: SecretAgent-Gradient optimizes the perturbation through six surrogate encoders for cross-model transferability, and the gradient-free SecretAgent-Tool composes procedural noise and achieves the best perceptual fidelity on three of the five datasets. Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.
item.dc:creator: Minda Zhao, Yue Zhang, Mengyu Wang

item.title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2611.26938v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Jun Zhang, Tong Qian, Hua Ding, Weijie Yu, Zhi-Hui Zhan

item.title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.26940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.
item.dc:creator: Bonny Banerjee, Geetha Raju

item.title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.26957v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.
item.dc:creator: Zijia Cao, Hanqing Dou

item.title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2611.26965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.
item.dc:creator: Anika Misra, Chimaobi Okite, Rada Mihalcea

item.title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.
item.dc:creator: Yao Tong, Jiaxin Qi, Yan Cui, Jinli Ou, Yuhua Zheng, Jianqiang Huang

item.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.26980v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
item.dc:creator: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov

item.title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.26983v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.
item.dc:creator: Zibin Lin, Taotao Wang, Shengli Zhang

item.title: JevRisk: Zero-Shot Financial Risk Assessment with a Language Decision Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.26999v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Banks must monitor every customer's financial risk, such as money laundering and credit default, by interpreting financial activity in the context of the customer's profile. Existing risk monitoring systems of banks are mostly based on expert-designed risk indicators, which apply predefined thresholds to every customer and cannot adapt to their personal situations. Supervised models recognise risk patterns from labelled customers, but each label often needs an expert's review or months of repayment history, which is slow and costly. Financial risk assessment therefore calls for a zero-shot decision system that minimises the need for labels and generalises across customers and risk types. To this end, we present JevRisk, a system for zero-shot financial risk assessment with a language decision model. JevRisk works in two steps. First, following regulatory guidelines in the finance domain, JevRisk computes exact risk indicators with code. Second, the language decision model (e.g., \jev{}) reads these indicators together with the customer's profile and activity, judges the case in context with broad world knowledge, and returns the score of high risk. We evaluate JevRisk on the anti-money laundering task with public synthetic data from Scotiabank and on the credit risk task with real data from Home Credit and Lending Club. On both tasks, JevRisk outperforms rule-based and unsupervised methods, and is on par with or better than supervised methods (e.g., GBDT and TabPFN) trained on about a thousand labelled customers.
item.dc:creator: Yaodong Yang, Li Huang, Junpeng Liang, Yi Ma, Hongyao Tang, Xingyu Fan, Jinpeng Li, Furui Liu

item.title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.27011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach-grasp and transport-placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach-grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Shuai Peng, Yongkai Liao, Yuxin Cheng, Haoyuan Wang, Jian Huang

item.title: Ruby: State-of-the-Art Potency Prediction across Discovery Regimes Using Learned Structural Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27015v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small-molecule drug discovery proceeds through repeated design-make-test-analyze cycles. The goal is often to maximize potency while keeping other properties within the ranges required for a viable therapeutic candidate. Compound prioritization places different demands on computational methods as drug discovery progresses from hit identification through hit-to-lead and lead optimization, with changing computational budgets and increasing amounts of on-target experimental data. We introduce Ruby, a Robust Universal Binding affinitY predictor that uses intermediate representations from the structural foundation model Pearl without requiring an explicit binding pose for every compound. Ruby is trained on proprietary data plus GenesisPotency-2026, an audited public-source potency training dataset released for academic and commercial use under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license with row-level provenance and audit annotations. Ruby achieves the highest aggregate early enrichment across seven public hit-identification targets among evaluated methods, with adjustable inference effort trading off enrichment and computational cost over more than two orders of magnitude. Ruby achieves the highest average correlations across four public benchmarks: OpenFE, CASP16, FEP+ 4, and OpenBind. Ruby significantly outperforms other methods in zero-shot prediction across eight biochemical and cellular assays from five ongoing Genesis-Incyte programs, widening its performance advantage relative to the public benchmarks. Ruby continues to improve more than other methods when all are given the opportunity to recalibrate using earlier assay measurements. Together, these contributions provide an annotated training resource for the field and a state-of-the-art potency predictor for broad screening, prioritization within related chemical series, and assay-specific prediction as experimental measurements accumulate.
item.dc:creator: Michael Atkin, Dominique Beaini, Jules Berman, Rebecca Boiarsky, Jamin Chen, Alejandro Dobles, Sergey Edunov, Evan Feinberg, Nate Gruver, Will Harvey, Deidre Johns, Nina Jovic, Steven Kearnes, Allison Keys, Rohit Kundu, Ken Leidal, Gerald Lelais, Michael V. Levine, Indrawan McAlpine, Gabriel Monteiro da Silva, Igor Morozov, Pranav Murugan, Adi Nagle, Frank Pickard, Wesley Qian, Gianluca Scarpellini, Ansh Sharma, Richard Strong Bowen, Wojtek Swiderski, Laura Tapias, Carl Tilbury, Cyr Vetcher, Han Wang, William Wang, David Charles Williams, Drausin Wulsin, Han Yoon

item.title: Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced Hierarchy-Aware Semi-Supervised Graph Classification
item.description: arXiv:2611.27043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semi-supervised graph classification aims to learn graph-level representations by leveraging a large number of unlabeled graphs alongside a small set of labeled ones, effectively mitigating the issue of label scarcity. Despite significant progress by various semi-supervised learning strategies, complex relationships among graph vertices beyond pairwise edges, especially hierarchical structures, remain underexplored by existing methods. In this work, we propose a Hypergraph Structural Entropy-Enhanced hierarchy-aware framework, namely HypSEE, for semi-supervised graph classification. Specifically, we first construct walk-induced and embedding-derived hypergraphs to capture hierarchy-aware local and long-range higher-order relationships within graphs. Then, we devise a hierarchical hypergraph pooling approach guided by hypergraph structural entropy (HSE) to facilitate hierarchical representation learning in hypergraphs. Lastly, we employ an anchor graph-based consistency strategy to mutually align the representations from these two hypergraph views, enhancing the learning efficacy on unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on 8 benchmark datasets demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Guangjie Zeng, Hao Peng, Angsheng Li, Li Sun, Chunyang Liu, Yicheng Pan, Shengze Li, Philip S. Yu

item.title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.27057v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.
item.dc:creator: Sujeet Lahane, Sapna Mishra, Akash Suryavanshi, Tapan Gandhi, Bharat Biswal

item.title: PACE: Policy Augmentation and Compensation With Explicit Disturbance Estimation for Robust Locomotion
item.description: arXiv:2611.27061v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning has made quadrupedal locomotion remarkably robust. To handle unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances, domain randomization is usually employed to make a policy hedge against every condition it might meet. However, maintaining accurate tracking across varying dynamics and generalizing beyond the sampled range remain challenging. Here we show that explicitly estimating the disturbance and feeding the resulting estimation back into both the policy and the controller can relax this compromise. We introduce Policy Augmentation and Compensation with Explicit disturbance estimation (PACE). The framework lumps payload variations, center-of-mass (CoM) shifts, actuator degradation, and external forces into one joint-space disturbance. A nonlinear observer subsequently recovers this disturbance online without requiring joint acceleration measurements. The disturbance estimation provides feedforward torque compensation as the foundational control pathway and further augments the policy observation to enable disturbance-aware action generation. Considering the learning difficulty of fast-varying contact effects, we further provide an analytical contact estimation approach from joint and inertial measurements, without demanding force sensors. Across eleven simulated dynamics conditions, PACE reduces velocity-tracking error by 18.1% to 57.0% against state-of-the-art baselines, and maintains improved tracking under out-of-distribution (OOD) commands. Notably, in real-world experiments, the deployed real robot carried an 11.5 kg payload, nearly equal to its own mass. It also negotiated unseen 16 cm step-downs and crossed five outdoor terrains. The policy was trained exclusively on flat ground in simulation with at most 3 kg of added mass.
item.dc:creator: Shixuan Han, Yuyang Wang, Jingting Jia, Zeshuai Chen, Jindou Jia, Kexin Guo, Xiang Yu

item.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
item.description: arXiv:2611.27079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.
item.dc:creator: Rapha\"el Bonnet-Guerrini, Johann Ioannou-Nikolaides, Troels Petersen

item.title: Fooling the Mind Twice: Human Detection of Audiovisual Deepfakes Under Repeated Exposure and Corrective Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2611.27080v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Human deepfake detection remains unreliable, and whether reassessment with corrective feedback improves subsequent judgments remains unclear. This study examined differences between initial and repeated deepfake assessments among 110 participants using audiovisual stimuli from the FakeAVCeleb and Deepfake Detection Challenge (DFDC) datasets. Participants evaluated 40 videos from each dataset in phase 1 (PhaseI) and reassessed the same videos in phase 2 (PhaseII) under a procedure combining repeated presentation and corrective feedback. For the FakeAVCeleb dataset, the participants' mean accuracy increased by 4.68 percentage points from 63.30 in PhaseI to 67.98 in PhaseII (t(109)=5.61, p<.001, d_z=0.54). A judgment-level logistic regression with standard errors clustered by participant and video produced a consistent result: beta=0.208, SE=0.040, z=5.23, p<.001, {OR}=1.23. For the DFDC dataset, the participants' mean accuracy increased by 8.64 percentage points from 59.52% in PhaseI to 68.16% in PhaseII (t(109)=7.37, p<.001, d_z=0.70); the logistic model yielded: beta=0.375, SE=0.065, z=5.78, p<.001, {OR}=1.46. Improvements primarily came from fewer false negatives, while false-positive rates remained unchanged. However, judgment reversals occurred in 27.55% of FakeAVCeleb and 32.91% of DFDC assessments, with some initially correct judgments becoming incorrect upon reassessment. Despite the accuracy gains, repeated assessment did not eliminate judgment instability or residual error. Participants also exhibited consistent overconfidence, with mean self-rated confidence exceeding actual accuracy by 11.99 percentage points for FakeAVCeleb and 12.82 percentage points for DFDC across both phases. These findings indicate that repetition with corrective feedback moderately improves deepfake detection but does not fully resolve the limitations of human judgment.
item.dc:creator: Ammarah Hashmi, Sahibzada Adil Shahzad, Yu Tsao, Hsin-Min Wang

item.title: Exercised, Rarely Recovered: What Public Reports Say About Recovery in 50 AI Agent Harnesses and Runtimes
item.description: arXiv:2611.27090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When an AI coding agent deletes the wrong files or a long agent run crashes, users fall back on recovery mechanisms: resume from a checkpoint, undo, ask for approval, read the log. Research runtimes promise stronger guarantees, such as saga-style compensation and transactional rollback. We ask what public evidence shows about whether either kind works in real use. Under a protocol frozen before data collection, we graded 12 persistent agent runtimes, 26 coding-agent harnesses and 12 research runtimes on eight recovery mechanisms, from not found to exercised in a real run, with two blind coding passes, adjudication and re-verification against archived sources. Recovery is exercised almost everywhere in practice: 11 of 12 runtimes and 25 of 26 harnesses have at least one real-use report. Yet of 128 such reports, only 19 describe the run fully recovering; 54 are partial and 45 failed. Checkpoint/resume recovered once in 27 reports, rollback once in 15. Research runtimes show the opposite profile: guarantees evaluated on benchmarks, none reported in operation, and compensation of external effects, their central guarantee, is offered by no harness at all.
item.dc:creator: Kaviru Hapuarachchi

item.title: Separating Automation Gains from Agent Contributions in AI-Assisted Model Validation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27094v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents are being proposed for bank model validation, yet evaluations that compare agent-assisted work with manual practice credit the agent with gains that come from digitized evidence and deterministic tests. We propose a staged architecture in which an LLM-free controlled workflow (P1) is both the fallback and the control arm for individually authorized agent tasks (P2), and an attribution protocol that credits an agent only for faults P1 does not already report. The protocol charges decoy false alarms, unnecessary actions and endorsed developer assertions, counts invalid outputs as misses, folds newly automatable findings back into P1 with discovery credit, and fixes safety bounds and a break-even cost gate in advance. On a synthetic credit-scorecard harness, five scripted reference policies show why this matters: naive case accuracy (4/6) and pooled detection (3/5) tie four flawed policies, whereas the protocol separates all five and credits only the reference policy with detection beyond P1. One fold-back round raises a P1-parroting policy's naive scores without any change to the policy. A regression matrix of sixteen mutants covers nine ways in which earlier versions of the evaluation passed misleadingly. No LLM agent has been evaluated yet; we specify a falsifiable pilot.
item.dc:creator: M. Ahmadi Achachlouei

item.title: Epistemic Guard: Out-of-Process MCP Receipt Proxying, Post-Turn Prose Supervision, and Provenance-Gated Memory for Tool-Using Autonomous Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.27095v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language-model agents using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) face three runtime verification gaps: (i) action fabrication, where post-tool prose narrates side effects that failed, timed out, or never ran; (ii) provenance collapse, where unverified model prose or web text enters durable memory alongside executed tool outputs; and (iii) syndicated echo amplification, where mirrored web pages satisfy multi-source corroboration from one origin. Existing MCP firewalls inspect wire calls before execution, while LLM-judge guardrails require multi-gigabyte VRAM without binding prose to receipts. We present epistemic-guard (v0.5.2), an open-source Python library and out-of-process stdio MCP receipt proxy (15 modules, 0 MiB GPU VRAM). epistemic-guard isolates Ed25519 signing keys out of process, writes RFC 6962 Merkle logs with AER-1 receipt translation, checks post-turn prose on CPU with SHA-256-verified OpenVINO INT8 encoders (4 models, 279.48 MB total; 82.67 MB on the supervision path), gates SQLite writes across 7 provenance domains, and collapses verbatim and lightly edited wire-syndicated RAG mirrors. On conformance suites, epistemic-guard rejects 100.0% of tampered receipts (200 Merkle leaves), passes 58/58 official AER-1 ingestion vectors and 50/50 reference-verified AER-1 exports, verifies 100.0% of 40 fault-injected wire calls and 100 concurrent appends with 0 key leaks, and blocks 100.0% of 100 unauthorized memory writes. Across $N=250$ frozen-benchmark traces, epistemic-guard reaches 93.2% accuracy at 17.9 ms warm median CPU latency (8.62 ms single-clause; 921.8 ms cold-start load), beating 12B-14B GPU judges by 6.4-6.8 points ($p=0.0259$, $p=0.0095$) at 4.26-4.5$\times$ lower latency; on $N=60$ live mcp-proxy traces, it catches 96.15% of hazards at 76.67% accuracy (38.24% FPR; $+18.34$ points over Stage-1-only, $p=0.001$) in 9.16 ms p50.
item.dc:creator: Sean Maxwell

item.title: One state, many questions: Opsis gives a frontier model typed eyes for pathology
item.description: arXiv:2611.27102v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A synoptic pathology report is a checklist of questions with fixed answer sets, many composed from others. Pathology foundation models answer them accurately with one classifier trained with labels for each, and frontier language models, which compose freely, cannot fit a slide of fourteen thousand tiles in their context. On 189 breast report questions, frontier models that read a written description of the slide or look at a thumbnail and tiles of it answer at 0.50 to 0.66, below the majority class at 0.67. A description is written before the question is known, and a look covers a handful of tiles. We present Opsis, which lets the model ask instead: a typed question interface on a frozen pathology encoder. A slide is encoded once, a question names an operator, arguments and candidates given at runtime, and the answer is a probability over the candidates. We build it as a 10 M parameter decoder on frozen Virchow2 tokens (Opsis-S) and inside Qwen3-VL-8B (Opsis-V). Asking Opsis-S, four frontier models answer the breast questions at 0.78 to 0.79, and on 3,797 pan cancer questions asking is 8.6 points above reading. On 995 composite questions that Opsis-S was never trained on, a frontier model composing its answers reaches 0.76, against 0.69 when it looks at the slide and 0.78 for ABMIL trained on each composite. On a pan cancer question set over 10,712 TCGA slides, one Opsis-S decoder matches linear probes trained per question on TITAN and PRISM2 embeddings (average accuracy 0.69 against 0.70 and 0.68). Opsis-S also separates CAMELYON16 metastases without training on that cohort (AUROC 0.86) and localises necrosis from report labels alone (tile AUROC 0.93).
item.dc:creator: Zhixuan Ge, Wei Qiu

item.title: Schema-Validated LLM Workflows: A Benchmark Protocol and Comparative Evaluation Across Six Python Implementations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to extract records, generate SQL, summarize reports, answer policy questions, and route operational work. At these software boundaries, parseable output is necessary but does not establish task correctness. We present a reproducible benchmark protocol, a public executable artifact, and a confirmatory live API evaluation that separate structural validity from task-specific correctness across five business workflow tasks and six Python implementation conditions: PydanticAI, LangGraph, DSPy, CrewAI, Agno, and a framework-free SDK reference. We hypothesize that (H1) schema validity and task quality are separable, (H2) structured-output binding paths are heterogeneous under a shared model and lowest-common-denominator contract, and (H3) condition-by-task interactions concentrate failures rather than shifting all tasks equally. Confirmatory analysis uses distinct task instances (100 extraction and 50 per other task, with three nested replicates) under a frozen analysis plan, yielding a 5400-row primary matrix with equivalence margins and Holm-adjusted contrasts against the SDK reference. In the eligible confirmatory run, overall schema validity was 0.684 and mean automated quality was 0.638. PydanticAI, LangGraph, and DSPy retained near-ceiling schema validity with mean quality 0.91-0.94, while the plain SDK, Agno, and CrewAI conditions were substantially lower in this package and model configuration. Schema-valid rows still produced many task-score flags, especially in extraction and compliance QA, and quality residuals show strong condition-by-task interactions (including a workflow collapse for CrewAI). Labelled ablations address retry budgets and feature-using mechanisms; primary contrasts remain system-configuration findings, not causal attributions to marketed library features.
item.dc:creator: Sidney Shapiro, Sanad Al-Khatib, Aurora Pinz\'on Arzola, Emiliano Sebastian Gonzalez Venegas, Daniel Pearson

item.title: Do Senior Agents Do Their Job? Measuring Role Integrity in How LLM Agents Use Subordinate Material
item.description: arXiv:2611.27139v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly divide long tasks among subagents whose reports a senior agent turns into the final answer. Such a division of labor pays off only if each agent, and above all the senior agent, carries out the duties of its role. Current evaluations, however, mostly score the final answer, and a fluent, well-cited answer cannot show whether the senior agent weighed its subagents' reports or merely aggregated them. To assess whether a senior agent meets its assigned responsibilities, we define role integrity as the preservation of an agent's functional responsibilities when it acts on its subordinates' material. To measure it, we introduce RI-Bench, a behavioral benchmark grounded in the structures and public records of three institutional hierarchies: peer review, appellate adjudication, and parliamentary inquiry. We choose these hierarchies because their rules explicitly assign the senior role a duty toward subordinate material, and together they cover three basic duties: to weigh, to verify, and to relay. Rather than scoring output correctness, we measure how senior agents' outputs respond to controlled changes in subordinate material, using rule-based checks and a rubric-guided LLM judge calibrated against human annotation. Across eight LLMs and over 12,000 agentic episodes, senior agents rarely adopt a planted procedural error (2.9% of rulings) but often follow a majority of generic reviews (up to 71% of decisions) or drop witnesses' stated limitations (up to 65% of cited claims). Obligation prompts reduce these failures without removing them, and they also shift behavior in the control conditions. These findings motivate direct, obligation-specific evaluation of role integrity rather than inferring it from general capability or explicit role instructions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jxtse/ri-bench.
item.dc:creator: Jinxiang Xie, Xinyi Zhang, Changjiang Jiang, Kexu Liu, Qi Yang, Yuxin Su

item.title: How Does SAM-3 Adapt? Capacity, Update Geometry, and Domain Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.27142v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Promptable segmentation foundation models are increasingly used in specialized domains, but it remains unclear how SAM-3 should be fine-tuned when adapting it beyond its original training distribution. We study this question by comparing five adaptation families --LoRA, HiRA, KRAdapter, QuanTA, and Full Fine-Tuning-- across five segmentation datasets spanning medical imaging, remote sensing, and dense material segmentation. Across these datasets, compact parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods often match or approach Full Fine-Tuning in DSC and IoU, suggesting that strong in-domain adaptation does not always require updating the full model. However, this performance cannot be explained by nominal adapter rank or trainable parameter count alone. To investigate why different methods perform similarly, we analyze their update spectra and their behavior under LoveDA Urban/Rural transfer. Our SVD analysis shows that Full Fine-Tuning updates are spectrally compressible. However, successful PEFT methods do not simply recover the same update directions; instead, they often concentrate changes in different components and subspaces. The domain-transfer study further shows that methods with similar in-domain performance can respond differently under distribution shift. Together, these results suggest that SAM-3 adaptation is often capacity-saturated in practice, while competitive fine-tuning arises through method-specific update paths rather than a single low-rank approximation to Full Fine-Tuning.
item.dc:creator: Allan Kazakov, Abdurrahman Javat, Duygu Cakir

item.title: Structure Over Scale: Rethinking Adaptation for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
item.description: arXiv:2611.27148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is often framed as a choice between the expressivity of Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) and the efficiency of Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We find that this framing misses an important variable: the geometry of the update. Under a common cold-start GRPO protocol, LoRA exhibits rank collapse: performance remains broadly stable at low rank, then fails abruptly as rank increases. On DeepMath-Hard, for example, accuracy drops from 73.1% at r=64 to 4.7% at r=128. In contrast, Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) and Quantum-Informed Tensor Adaptation (QuanTA) remain stable over a wider tested optimization region and are competitive with FFT while updating less than 0.6% of the model parameters. Spectral analysis reveals a corresponding difference in learned update structure: collapsed LoRA concentrates its update energy into relatively few effective directions, whereas structured adapters produce substantially more distributed updates. These results suggest that nominal rank and parameter count alone are insufficient to characterize adaptation in RLVR - the structure imposed on the reachable update manifold also matters. Finally, across three 8B base models, adapter behavior aligns with both frozen-weight spectral structure and reported pre-training scale, motivating the Model Maturity Hypothesis: the adaptation geometry that works best may depend on properties already encoded during pre-training. We present this as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than a causal conclusion. The code can be found here https://github.com/Shrimpstanot/structure-over-scale
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), October 2026
item.dc:creator: Allan Kazakov, Abdurrahman Javat

item.title: Co-Evolving Behavioral Agents and Detectors for Adaptive Information Operations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27156v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Detectors of state-sponsored information operations (IOs) are trained on campaigns that platforms have already taken down. They lose much of their accuracy on an actor they have not seen, even though no operator in the archived data is trying to avoid them. A real operator wants two things, to reach an audience and to avoid being caught. We present IO-AI, a framework that gives simulated agents these two capabilities, engagement and evasion, and tests what each one does to detection.
